1720	The man stole on Shabbat. Now he comes on a weekday to return the money, repenting of the theft. He
1721	doesn't give him 600 shekels, the principal. He gives him 1,000, which is also the price of what?
1722	Of the profit.
1723	But on Shabbat, it is forbidden to benefit from Shabbat earnings.
1724	Maybe he also suffered damage...
1725	Are you allowed to take a thousand now, or six hundred? You take the principal from him.
1726	Maybe he also suffered damage from the break-in.
1727	There was no damage.
1728	What do you do in such a case?
1729	Will it be permitted to you or forbidden?
1730	What do you say?
1731	What do you do about insurance, or damages?
1732	He will be permitted to take the principal.
1733	The answer: if he pays him on Shabbat, it is Shabbat earnings and forbidden.
1734	But if he pays him after Shabbat, he comes on a weekday.
1735	The thief did not come to him on Shabbat itself.
1736	He came to him on a weekday, after Shabbat.
1737	On a weekday.
1738	So it is permitted to you, as if he stole it on a weekday, and bought it on a weekday.
1739	Only if he could have bought it on a weekday.
1740	Only if he pays on Shabbat, then you are forbidden to take it.
1741	Because then you are receiving the act of theft that you had.
1742	The question now is: on Shabbat itself, when he comes to pay, must he take the six hundred?
1743	Or will you lose even the six hundred?
1744	And here there was an incident with the gaon Rabbi Eilan of Kolmi, may the memory of the tzaddik be a blessing.
1745	Once on Shabbat he is sitting and learning Torah.
1746	Suddenly he sees a hand above his head, hovering.
1747	The Rabbi is sitting at home learning Torah, and a hand is hovering over his head.
1748	It is trying to reach the wallets with the money.
1749	That same hand, he shouted...
1750	He looks, raises his eyes, and sees a thief.
1751	He says to him: wallets are muktzeh, why are you touching them?
1752	The thief laughs, takes the wallet, and takes the other one too.
1753	Credit cards, from one of them.
1754	The Rabbi shouts at him: it is written, "You shall not steal!"
1755	It's not only muktzeh, it's theft.
1756	The thief laughed, grabbed the two wallets, one in his right hand and one in his left, snatched the wallets,
1757	and ran off.
1758	As he flees, the Rabbi shouts at him: But my wife!
1759	She'll be distressed over this. Don't you care about the distress of my wife? What a distress for my wife.
